  - Comprehensive software for continuous 360° visual monitoring and inspection of high‑performance steel wire ropes, integrating visual inspection with third‑party magneto‑inductive testing (MRT).   - Bart Blockmans — Senior Algorithms Developer; PhD in computational mechanics (KU Leuven). ([raidyn.ai](https://www.raidyn.ai/about-us?utm_source=openai))

  - Board: Ben Schrauwen (ex‑Professor of Machine Learning; industry leadership at Autodesk, 3D Systems, Oqton) and Samir Hanna (PhD in Numerical Simulation; former Autodesk SVP for Manufacturing and Simulation). ([raidyn.ai](https://www.raidyn.ai/about-us?utm_source=openai))

- Partnerships
  - AIM Consortium (Alliance for Intelligent Rope Monitoring) with Teufelberger‑Redaelli and AMC Instruments, combining MRT, cameras, and AI to detect broken wires, corrosion, and geometric issues; delivers automatic, customizable reports to reduce downtime and enable predictive maintenance. ## Summary

Raidyn is a Leuven-based deep-tech company building AI-driven inspection and monitoring software for mission-critical engineering components. Its current public focus is steel wire rope monitoring through a product called **AURA**.

## Current State

- Public company launch appears to be recent, with third-party sources placing the company in 2024.
- The current public product focus is continuous **360° visual monitoring and inspection of steel wire ropes**.
- Raidyn presents its approach as a hybrid of **AI, computer vision, edge computing, and simulation-based modeling**.
- Public materials indicate early real-world deployments, several orders, and a growing pipeline, but exact customer counts and revenue are not public in the sources reviewed.

## Offering

- **AURA**: Automatic Rope Analysis / rope monitoring software.
- Core capabilities described publicly:
  - continuous 360° visual inspection
  - lay-length and diameter analysis
  - historical condition tracking
  - real-time monitoring from the control room
  - automatic and customizable reporting
  - integration with third-party magneto-inductive rope testing (**MRT**)
- Deployment posture:
  - designed to run on edge hardware
  - public references mention NVIDIA Jetson hardware
  - website positioning suggests local/industrial deployment rather than cloud-first monitoring

## Target Problems And Value

Raidyn's public messaging centers on:

- earlier detection of rope damage and degradation
- improved safety for mission-critical assets
- reduced downtime
- better inspection consistency and traceability
- support for predictive maintenance decisions

## Focus Industries

Publicly listed applications include:

- cableways
- mining
- offshore drilling
- construction

Raidyn describes its technical edge as a combination of:

- applied AI
- computer vision
- hybrid simulation-data methods
- probabilistic performance models
- resource-efficient edge computing for industrial hardware

## Partnerships And Ecosystem

- Raidyn publicly presents the **AIM Consortium** / **Alliance for Intelligent Rope Monitoring** together with:

  - **AMC Instruments**

Here’s what you need to read Figma files via the REST API with a Personal Access Token (PAT) as of March 16, 2026:

Required scopes for “read file” use cases
- File JSON or node data: file_content:read (used by GET /v1/files/:key, /v1/files/:key/nodes, and /v1/images/:key). ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/file-endpoints/))
- File metadata only (no document content): file_metadata:read (GET /v1/files/:key/meta). ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/file-endpoints/))
- Read comments (if needed): file_comments:read. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/scopes/))
- Identify the calling user (optional): current_user:read. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/scopes/))
- Note: files:read is now deprecated—use the granular scopes above instead. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/scopes/))

Access and sharing (who can the PAT see?)
- Scopes don’t override sharing/permissions. The PAT can only access files that the PAT owner’s Figma account can access (because they created the file, were invited, or have team/project access). ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/scopes/))
- Granting access: invite the PAT owner’s email to the file/project/team with Can view, or configure link sharing per your org’s policy. Viewer access is sufficient for read-only endpoints. ([help.figma.com](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040531773-Share-files-and-prototypes?utm_source=openai))

Viewer vs. editor and rate limits
- Seat type affects API limits. View/Collab seats can be heavily constrained (e.g., Tier 1 endpoints like GET file can be limited to “up to 6 per month” on Starter plans), while Dev/Full seats get higher per‑minute limits. For automations, ensure the PAT owner has an appropriate seat on the plan that hosts the file. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/rate-limits/?utm_source=openai))

Token creation and usage
- Create a PAT in Settings → Security; choose scopes and an expiration, then send it in the X-Figma-Token header. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/authentication/?utm_source=openai))
- Since April 28, 2025, PATs can have a maximum expiry of 90 days—plan for rotation. Also, “Projects” endpoints now require approval. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/changelog/?utm_source=openai))

Quick checklist
- Give the PAT owner at least “Can view” access to the target file (or appropriate inherited access). ([help.figma.com](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040531773-Share-files-and-prototypes?utm_source=openai))
- Request only the scopes you need (file_content:read and/or file_metadata:read, plus any others your workflow requires). ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/scopes/))
- Consider seat/plan rate limits for your use case. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/rate-limits/?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me exactly what you want to read (full document JSON, specific nodes, images, comments, or just metadata), I can list the minimal scopes and example requests for that flow. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/file-endpoints/))

Details (most common read‑only scopes for “files”):
- file_content:read — required for GET /v1/files/:key, GET /v1/images/:key, and GET /v1/files/:key/images. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/file-endpoints/?utm_source=openai))
- file_metadata:read — read file metadata without content (GET /v1/files/:key/meta). ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/file-endpoints/?utm_source=openai))
- file_versions:read — read a file’s version history. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/version-history-endpoints/?utm_source=openai))
- file_comments:read — read comments on a file. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/comments-endpoints/?utm_source=openai))

How to request scopes in OAuth:
- Pass them in the oauth authorize URL (comma- or space‑separated), e.g. scope=file_content:read,file_metadata:read. ([developers.figma.com](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/authentication/?utm_source=openai))

- The broad files:read/file_read scopes were deprecated and removed in favor of granular scopes like file_content:read and file_metadata:read; migrating to their granular equivalents doesn’t require user re‑auth if they’re a subset. Yes — with one important limit:

I can help you **read and analyze Figma content**, but I can’t personally “log into Figma like a human” from here unless you give this workspace a machine-readable way to access it.

## Best ways to do it

### Option 1: Safest and simplest
Export the important material from Figma into this workspace.

Good exports:
- PDF exports of key flows
- PNG screenshots of important frames
- copied text from strategy, product, sales, or design pages
- FigJam exports
- component library docs
- board screenshots with annotations

Put them in:
- `inbox/figma/`

Then I can:
- read them
- summarize what Raidyn is, how the product works, key user flows, design language, open questions
- update the right company and work-item records

This is the **lowest-risk** option.

---

### Option 2: Read-only Figma API access
If you want me to inspect Figma more directly, you can give this workspace a **read-only Figma API token**.

## What you would need
Create a Figma personal access token with the smallest useful scopes:

- `file_content:read`
- `file_metadata:read`

Optional if you want deeper context:
- `file_comments:read`
- `file_versions:read`

Also:
- the Figma account that owns the token must already have access to the files
- viewer access is enough for read-only use

## Important security note
Do **not** paste a token into chat if you want to avoid it being stored in conversation history.

Better:
- store it in a local non-committed env file like `.env.local`
- or in a local shell session environment variable
- and give me the file links or file keys

## Then I can help by
- fetching file metadata
- reading file structure and page names
- extracting frames/nodes/images
- identifying product flows, screens, terminology, personas, and design-system clues
- turning that into clean internal records for Raidyn

---

## What I cannot promise
Even with full read-only Figma access, I still won’t “know everything” about Raidyn.

Figma is great for:
- product flows
- UX decisions
- messaging
- internal boards
- roadmaps
- sales or investor decks if they live there

But it won’t fully replace:
- internal docs
- CRM/pipeline context
- customer conversations
- roadmap decisions
- company strategy notes

So Figma is **very useful**, but not the whole picture.

---

## My recommendation
Use this order:

1. Give me the **top 3–10 most important Figma files**
2. Start with either:
   - exports in `inbox/figma/`, or
   - a read-only API token
3. I produce:
   - a Raidyn context brief
   - a product and stakeholder summary
   - a list of gaps and assumptions
   - updates to `entities/companies/co-raidyn/record.md`

---

## If you want the API route, here’s the clean setup
You can do something like this locally:

1. Create a read-only Figma token
2. Save it in `.env.local`:
```bash
FIGMA_TOKEN=your_token_here
```

3. Give me the Figma file links you want analyzed

Then I can help with the rest.

---

## If you want, I can do one of these next
1. give you a **step-by-step Figma token setup**
2. give you a **safe folder structure for Figma exports**
3. give you a **small script** to pull read-only Figma data into this workspace
4. help you choose **which Figma files to share first**

My recommendation is **3 + 4** if you want the smoothest setup.

Here’s the up-to-date picture (as of March 16, 2026) for a Slack app that needs to read channel history and look up users.

Reading message history (use conversations.history)
- Required scopes depend on conversation type:
  - Public channels: channels:history
  - Private channels: groups:history
  - Direct messages: im:history
  - Group DMs: mpim:history
- Token access rules:
  - App/bot tokens can read conversations they’re a member of, with the relevant *:history scope.
  - User tokens can read all public channels and any private conversations the user is a member of, with the relevant *:history scope. ([api.slack.com](https://api.slack.com/methods/conversations.history?utm_source=openai))

Listing or discovering conversations (often needed to find channel IDs)
- Use Conversations API (e.g., conversations.list). Scopes act as filters:
  - channels:read, groups:read, im:read, mpim:read — add the ones matching the conversation types you care about. ([api.slack.com](https://api.slack.com/apis/conversations-api?utm_source=openai))
- A simple “public channels only” setup commonly uses channels:read + channels:history. ([api.slack.com](https://api.slack.com/messaging/retrieving?utm_source=openai))

Looking up users (users.info)
- Scope to read basic user objects: users:read
- To receive the email field, you must also request users:read.email. ([api.slack.com](https://api.slack.com/methods/users.info?utm_source=openai))

Rate limits you should plan around in 2026
- For non‑Marketplace apps, conversations.history and conversations.replies are limited to 1 request/minute and limit=15 for apps created after May 29, 2025, and for all existing external installs starting September 2, 2025. Internal apps created after May 29, 2025 can request increases from Slack. ([api.slack.com](https://api.slack.com/changelog/2025-05-terms-rate-limit-update-and-faq?utm_source=openai))

Want me to suggest the minimal scope set for your exact use case (public-only vs all conversation types, bot vs user token)?

Here’s the up‑to‑date picture (as of March 16, 2026) of Slack data export options and what each includes.

Plans and what you can export
- Public channels (standard export): Available on all plans. Exports include message text and links to files from public channels; on Free, file links are limited to the last 90 days. ([slack.com](https://slack.com/help/articles/201658943-Export-your-workspace-data?utm_source=openai))
- All channels and DMs (often called “corporate” export): On Business+ and Enterprise, an owner can apply for access to a self‑serve tool to export messages and file links from public channels, private channels, and DMs (including Slackbot). Approval is required. ([slack.com](https://slack.com/help/articles/201658943-Export-your-workspace-data?utm_source=openai))
- Enterprise extras: Org Owners can request additional options, including custom exports by conversation type, member, or specific workspace; per‑user exports (JSON or TXT); and a channel audit (CSV). ([slack.com](https://slack.com/help/articles/201658943-Export-your-workspace-data?utm_source=openai))

# Workspace Self-Improvement

- Use this guidance when improving Hermit itself: runtime code, prompts, entity definitions, scaffold templates, explorer renderers, validation, docs, tests, or operating guidance.

## Triggers

- The user explicitly asks to improve Hermit or its workflow.
- A correction, failed attempt, or repeated manual fix reveals a reusable gap.
- Telemetry shows repeated errors, retries, slow turns, or silent turns.
- `doctor` finds missing files, placeholder drift, or broken prompt links.
- The same fix keeps landing by hand in prompts, templates, renderers, or code.

## Choose The Layer

- `prompts/` for shared operating guidance.
- `{{roleRoot}}/prompts/` or `{{roleRoot}}/AGENTS.md` for role-local behavior.
- `src/` for deterministic runtime behavior, validation, scaffolding, or tool wiring.
- `entity-defs/` for default canonical structure.
- Explorer renderers for clearer read-only views.
- Docs and tests when a contract or regression boundary should be explicit.

## Loop

1. Read the smallest relevant canonical files first.
2. Gather evidence from user corrections, telemetry, `doctor`, failing tests, or repeated real-world friction.
3. Classify the change before editing.
4. Make the narrowest fix that addresses the root cause without weakening the file-first model.
5. If a contract changes, update adjacent docs, templates, manifests, or tests in the same pass.
6. Validate with the best available checks.
7. Capture unfinished follow-ups in `{{roleRoot}}/agent/inbox.md` or `{{roleRoot}}/agent/record.md`.

## Guardrails

- Preserve the file-first operating model.
- Keep shared and role-local responsibilities distinct.
- Do not replace explicit manifests, templates, or renderer mappings with hidden heuristics.
- Do not weaken evidence handling, source discipline, ambiguity checks, or privacy boundaries just to make self-improvement feel more automatic.
- Prefer repeated patterns over isolated impressions.
- Favor small, testable improvements over broad rewrites.
